local_facts.title: Atlanta's pollen count broke its record in March 2025
local_facts.claim: On Saturday 29 March 2025 Atlanta Allergy & Asthma recorded a pollen count of 14,801 grains per cubic meter of air, shattering the previous record of 9,368 set in March 2012. Any count above 1,500 is classed as extreme. Trees were the main source, after a warm February with no hard freeze brought an early bloom and a warm, dry March intensified it. The count is taken from a rooftop sampler and read under a microscope.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Pollen gets into a house through doors, windows and any return duct that pulls air from the attic or crawlspace. A filter that fits its slot catches most of it; a leaky return or a loose filter lets it reach the supply runs. Cleaning in the middle of a season like that is wasted money. Fix the filter and the leaks, then clean after the counts fall.

local_facts.title: Georgia has tested new duct systems for leaks since 2011
local_facts.claim: Georgia's state energy code took effect on 1 January 2011, and duct and envelope tightness (DET) verification became mandatory on new homes from 30 June 2011. A newly installed duct system must be tested if any part of it, or the air handler, sits outside the building envelope, in an unconditioned attic or crawlspace. As first written, the rules also required an existing system to pass the same test if more than half of it was modified, and required mastic on new or modified ductwork. Under Georgia's amendments to the 2015 IECC the duct leakage target is 6 CFM per 100 square feet of conditioned floor area, and testing must be done by a certified DET verifier such as a HERS rater or BPI analyst.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A Marietta house built before mid-2011 was never held to a duct leakage test, and its attic and crawlspace returns often pull dust, insulation fibers and humid air straight into the system. Cleaning those ducts without sealing them buys a few clean months, and the leak is usually the better use of the money.

local_facts.title: Georgia's extension service names the AC as a moisture source
local_facts.claim: University of Georgia Extension Circular 1047-1, Preventing Mold in Your Home (fully reviewed 1 March 2023), advises keeping indoor relative humidity below 60 percent and ideally between 30 and 50 percent. It lists air conditioning system flaws, naming an oversized unit, duct leaks, dirty coils and condensation, among the sources of excess moisture in a house, and recommends sealing leaks in HVAC ducts and the return plenum and running a well maintained, right-sized air conditioner with the fan on auto.
local_facts.why_it_matters: In a humid Georgia summer the indoor coil sits cold and wet for months, and that is where musty smells and growth usually start, not in the duct runs. A fan left on 'on' re-wets the house with water from the coil. The coil, the drain pan and the leaks deserve attention before anyone sells a duct sanitizer.

local_facts.title: Five historic districts of houses built before central air
local_facts.claim: The City of Marietta lists five National Register historic districts: Atlanta-Frasier Street, Church-Cherokee Street, Northwest Marietta, Washington Avenue and Whitlock Avenue, and in August 2013 part of Kennesaw Avenue became the city's first locally designated historic district. The Whitlock Avenue district, listed in 1989, covers 82 acres and 101 contributing buildings dating from before the Civil War into the 1930s. The Northwest Marietta district, listed in 1975, takes in about 230 acres of houses built roughly from the 1840s to the 1890s.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Almost none of those houses were built with forced air or central cooling. Most of their ductwork was added later, threaded through crawlspaces, closets and attics around plaster walls and old framing, and it is often a patchwork of metal and flexible duct of different ages. A cleaning there starts with finding where the runs actually go.
